Actually here

Twenty-five minutes east of NW 36th Street

We do not have an office in Doral. Appsurd works from 2125 Biscayne Blvd, in the corridor between Downtown Miami and the Design District, and that is the only address we have. Doral is roughly fifteen miles west — call it twenty-five minutes on the Dolphin outside of rush hour, and considerably more at 5pm, which anyone who commutes NW 36th Street already knows.

That matters because a lot of the firms ranking for "app development Doral" are running a national landing page with a mail-drop address in one of the office parks off NW 87th Avenue. It's a legal way to run a funnel. It is not a team you can get in a room. We would rather tell you the drive time than pretend we're around the corner.

For logistics and warehouse work, being in the same county is worth more than it sounds. Half of what goes wrong with a warehouse app is physical: the scanner gun someone actually issues to pickers, the dead spot in the middle of a metal building, the printer that only speaks ZPL, the driver who is not going to log in twice. We come to your facility, walk the process with the people doing it, and test on the hardware you own instead of the phone in the engineer's pocket.

Day-to-day delivery is still remote and asynchronous, because that's what a 48-hour cadence requires. But kickoff, floor walkthroughs and the arguments about how the data model should handle partial shipments are better in person, and we drive out for those.

The market

A city built on freight and paperwork

Doral is not a smaller Miami. It is a specific kind of place: a city of warehouses, showrooms, customs brokers, back-office headquarters and a very large Latin American business community, wrapped around the western edge of Miami International Airport.

The scale is real. The City of Doral counts more than 2,600 trade and logistics companies, over 250 company headquarters, more than 100 multinationals and over 50 banking and financial institutions inside about fifteen square miles. The FIU-prepared City of Doral Economic Analysis Report put the city at 4,626 business establishments employing 51,329 people, with wholesale trade the single largest sector at 8,612 workers and transportation and warehousing second at 6,500.

The airport next door is the engine. MIA handled a record 3.4 million tons of freight in 2025, up 13.2% year over year, against $89 billion in origin-and-destination trade value, and 85% of that freight was international. When a forwarder in Doral tells you a system outage costs them money by the hour, they are not being dramatic.

The workforce composition follows. Census figures compiled by Census Reporter show 11.5% of employed Doral residents working in transportation and warehousing against 8.4% countywide, and 6.6% in wholesale trade against 2.9% countywide. Seventy percent of residents are foreign born.

And the language of business is Spanish. About 41% of Doral residents are of Venezuelan origin — some 32,000 people — and 87.5% of residents speak Spanish at home, per the same ACS data. The City's own profile puts Spanish at 89%. Practically, that means a warehouse app with an English-only interface will be used badly, and an internal tool whose error messages only make sense in English will generate support calls instead of solving them.

The corporate layer is the part outsiders miss. Doral is where a long list of large employers keep their offices — the City lists Carnival, Perry Ellis International, Univision, Brink's, Hellmann Worldwide Logistics, Amadeus North America, AerSale, Badia Spices and Leon Medical Centers among them — and U.S. Southern Command is headquartered at 9301 NW 33rd St in Doral. One caveat worth stating plainly, because vendors keep getting it wrong: Carnival Corporation has been in Doral since the 1980s but broke ground on a new global headquarters campus at 887 Carnival Place in the Waterford Business District, which WLRN reported is expected to be complete in 2028. Doral's tenant list moves.

Districts

Where the work comes from

Doral reads as one grid of office parks from the highway. On the ground the brief changes noticeably depending on which corridor it comes from.

NW 36th Street & the cargo corridor

Freight forwarders, customs brokers, ground handlers, perishables. Work here is documentation and status: house and master bills, ACE/AMS filings, temperature logs, and shipment visibility that a client in Bogotá can check without calling anyone.

Beacon Lakes & west Doral industrial parks

Big-box distribution and 3PL space out toward the Everglades edge. Warehouse management, receiving, cycle counts, labour tracking — all of it on scanner hardware inside tilt-wall buildings where Wi-Fi coverage is a floor plan problem, not an IT preference.

Downtown Doral

Mixed-use offices and residential around NW 53rd Street. Corporate back-office briefs: approval workflows, vendor onboarding, internal reporting, and the dashboards a regional director shows a parent company in another country.

The tile & building products district

Doral bills itself as the country's #1 tile district, and the surrounding showrooms move stone, cabinetry, fixtures and finishes. Catalogue data, lot and dye-lot tracking, quoting tools, contractor portals, and images that have to be colour-accurate.

NW 87th Avenue office spine

Banking, insurance, professional services and Latin American regional offices. Integration work over systems nobody will replace, plus the compliance and audit-trail requirements that come with money moving across borders.

Doral Golf / hotel row

Resorts, conference and event business, and the food service around it. Group booking, event operations, staff scheduling, and demand that swings hard around the trade-show calendar.

Medley & the Okeechobee corridor

Heavier industry just north: aggregates, recycling, truck yards, cold storage. Yard management, gate check-in, driver dispatch and weight tickets, usually replacing carbon-copy forms.

County government campus

Miami-Dade police and fire-rescue facilities sit in Doral. Public-sector adjacent work with formal procurement, accessibility requirements and no tolerance for improvisation — the same shape as our Supreme Court of Ohio engagement.

Industries

Where the Doral budgets actually are

Ranked roughly by how often the brief reaches us from a Doral zip code. Almost none of it is a consumer app.

01

Freight forwarding & customs brokerage

The defining Doral industry and our most common brief here. Shipment files, house and master bills of lading, customs filings, arrival notices, document packs a client can download without emailing an agent. The recurring technical problem is that the source of truth is split across a forwarding system, a shared mailbox and a spreadsheet, so the first job is usually reconciliation rather than new features. Anything customer-facing also needs to be bilingual, because the shipper is frequently in Latin America.

02

Warehousing, 3PL & distribution

Receiving, putaway, picking, cycle counts, labour productivity, client-facing inventory portals. The hard part is not the interface, it's the hardware and the building: cheap Android scanner guns two or three OS versions behind, dead zones in the middle of racking, gloves, cold rooms and a network that drops. We build these offline-first with a local queue and explicit conflict handling, because a picker cannot stop working while the app waits for signal.

03

Import/export & LatAm wholesale trade

Doral is where goods are bought for a continent. Quoting, purchase orders, container consolidation, landed-cost calculation, multi-currency price lists and B2B ordering portals for buyers in a dozen countries. Tax IDs, phone formats and address rules vary by country, and pretending otherwise produces a validation layer that rejects real customers.

04

Trucking, drayage & last mile

Driver apps, dispatch, proof of delivery, ELD-adjacent workflows, yard and gate check-in. Driver adoption is the whole project: if the app takes more taps than the paper it replaced, it will be filled in at the end of the shift from memory, and your data is fiction. We design for one-handed use, large targets, photo capture and signature, and we test with drivers before we ship.

05

Aviation, aerospace & MRO

Doral's employer list includes aviation names like AerSale, KLX and B/E Aerospace, and the parts trade around MIA is substantial. Serialised inventory, traceability and certification documents, repair orders, quoting against AOG deadlines. Traceability requirements mean the audit trail is a product requirement, not a logging preference.

06

Corporate HQ & shared services

With 250-plus headquarters in the city, a lot of the work is internal: approval chains, vendor and contractor onboarding, expense and commission workflows, and reporting that rolls a Latin American region up to a parent company somewhere else. These projects live or die on integration with the ERP already in place, and on whether the reporting numbers match finance's numbers exactly.

07

Building products, tile & construction supply

Showroom and distribution businesses with deep catalogues and physical inventory. Product data management, quote-to-order, contractor and designer portals, sample and job tracking. Image fidelity and stock accuracy carry the experience — a beautiful catalogue app that shows an item as available when it isn't creates more work than it saves.

08

Spanish-language media, marketing & healthcare

Univision and Telefutura keep operations in Doral, and clinics like Leon Medical Centers serve a largely Spanish-speaking patient base. Content workflow, scheduling, patient intake and portals — with Spanish written natively rather than translated, and with HIPAA shaping the build wherever patient data is involved.

The hard part

Engineering for the warehouse floor

Most software failures we're asked to fix in Doral are not design failures. They are physics and hardware failures, and they show up in a predictable order.

The device is not your phone. The realistic target is a $180 Android handheld or a rugged scanner running an old OS, sometimes with a hardware scan trigger and a keyboard-wedge barcode driver, sometimes with a Bluetooth sled. That constrains the stack: no assumptions about modern browser APIs, no fifteen-megabyte JavaScript bundle, no camera-only scanning when a laser trigger is what the picker's hand already knows. We test on the actual model you issue, and we ask for one at kickoff.

The signal will drop. Tilt-wall construction, steel racking, cold rooms and freight elevators all eat Wi-Fi. Offline-first is not a feature to add later — it changes the data model. Writes get queued locally, every record needs an identity generated on the device, and someone has to decide what happens when two people count the same bin. We make that decision explicit at design time and write it into the spec, because the alternative is silent data loss discovered at inventory.

The paperwork is the product. In freight, the app usually exists to produce a document: a bill of lading, an arrival notice, a delivery receipt, a customs pack. That means label printers, PDF generation, page-perfect layouts, and EDI where trading partners require it. EDI in particular is a discipline rather than a feature — the standard is only half the work and the partner's interpretation of it is the other half, which is why we scope integration per partner instead of quoting "EDI" as one line.

The user did not ask for this. Drivers, pickers and dock staff are usually the last people consulted and the first people blamed. We build for them: Spanish-first interfaces, big targets, few taps, no scroll-to-find, and a workflow that mirrors what they already do physically. If the app is slower than the clipboard, it loses, and every metric you were going to report on becomes worthless.

Cost

What app development costs in Doral

Real ranges from real engagements, not a calculator built to capture your email. Every range includes design, engineering, QA and deployment — not engineering alone.

What you're buildingTypical rangeTime to launchWhen this is the right scope
Validation MVP$15k – $35k4 – 8 weeksOne workflow, one warehouse, one customer. Best used to prove that staff will actually use it before you fund the platform.
Driver or warehouse app$40k – $110k2 – 4 monthsAndroid-first, offline queue, barcode scanning, photo and signature capture, admin surface. The most common Doral brief we get.
Client-facing shipment visibility portal$55k – $150k3 – 5 monthsTracking, documents, notifications and bilingual accounts for shippers and consignees, on top of the system you already run.
Internal operations platform$60k – $180k3 – 6 monthsReplacing spreadsheets and WhatsApp across receiving, dispatch, billing and reporting for an operating business. Where most Doral budget goes.
Integration & EDI work$15k – $60k per system3 – 10 weeks eachForwarding or WMS systems, ERP, carrier APIs, EDI 214/315/856 and partner-specific variants. Priced per system because the cost is set by their documentation, not ours.
AI feature inside an existing product$25k – $90k4 – 10 weeksDocument extraction from commercial invoices and packing lists, retrieval over tariff and procedure documents, exception triage. Usually lands on top of software that already exists.
Productized squad (retainer)From $4,995/moFirst delivery in 48 hrsContinuous work with shifting priorities across several small tools. Unlimited requests, pause anytime, no change orders.
Ongoing maintenance$1.5k – $6k/mo—OS and store policy updates, dependency and security patches, monitoring, small changes. Android fleet fragmentation makes this less optional here than elsewhere.

Four things move a Doral number more than anything else. Hardware — supporting one known scanner model is cheap; supporting a mixed fleet of four generations of device is a testing matrix and a real line item. Offline behaviour — genuine offline-first with conflict resolution typically adds 20–35% over an online-only build, and it is the wrong thing to defer. Trading-partner integrations — each EDI partner or carrier API is its own small project, priced separately for a reason. Spanish at parity — cheap when designed in, expensive when retrofitted.

One thing that reduces the number: shrinking scope to a single facility and a single shift before rolling out. We would rather ship one working process to one building in six weeks than a platform to five buildings in eight months. Staff augmentation: our engineers embed in your repo, your standups, your Jira. You keep ownership of architecture and process; we add throughput without a 3–6 month hiring cycle.

Advisory and AI implementation: a fixed-scope audit that ends in an architecture, a build plan and a real number — not a slide deck. From $4,995.

Stack

What we build with, and why

Deliberately boring choices at the infrastructure layer, aggressive ones at the AI layer. Boring infrastructure is what lets a small team maintain a large surface area.

Swipe the table sideways to see all 3 columns →
LayerWhat we useWhy this and not something else
MobileReact Native (Expo), Swift / SwiftUI, KotlinReact Native when one codebase should serve both stores — most business apps. Native when the product depends on the camera, Bluetooth, background location, or hardware the bridge handles badly.
WebNext.js, React, TypeScript, TailwindServer rendering matters for anything that needs to be found in search, and TypeScript catches at compile time the class of bug that otherwise shows up in a store review.
BackendNode / TypeScript, Python for ML paths, PostgresOne language across client and server means one team can own the whole feature. Postgres because relational data is still relational, and because it will outlive whatever is fashionable this year.
InfrastructureVercel, AWS, Supabase, CloudflareManaged platforms until scale genuinely demands otherwise. Paying for infrastructure you can't operate is a slower failure than paying for one you can.
AI layerOpenAI, Anthropic, embeddings + retrieval, agent orchestrationAs an official OpenAI partner we build retrieval and agent workflows as first-class product features, not a chatbot bolted onto a finished app.
DeliveryGitHub, CI on every commit, staging per branch, SentryEvery increment is deployed and reviewable, which is the only way a 48-hour cadence stays honest instead of becoming a demo.

The full picture, including how we evaluate a new tool before it touches client work, is on the stack page. How we handle client data and access is documented on the security page.

Getting started

What the first two weeks look like

A Doral engagement usually starts with a thirty-minute call and, if the work touches a facility, a visit. We want to watch a receiving shift or ride along on a route rather than read a requirements document about one.

Within two business days you get a written scope: the build shape, the stack, the hardware assumptions, the integrations we can see, the risks, and a cost range. That document is yours whether you hire us or not. Several people have used ours to brief someone else, which is fine — an accurate scope is worth more to this corridor than a signed bad one.

If you go ahead, kickoff is day one and the first deployed increment lands inside 48 hours. You get the repo, the staging URL and access to everything from the start. For warehouse and driver work we aim to put something in a real user's hands inside the first two weeks, because their reaction is the only requirements document that has ever been reliable.
